name: Cori disease (glycogen storage disease type III)

reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Scriver's Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive disorder caused by deficiency of the glycogen debranching enzyme (AGL gene), leading to accumulation of abnormal, short-branched glycogen (limit dextrin)
Presents in childhood with fasting ketotic hypoglycaemia and prominent hepatomegaly, often resembling a milder von Gierke disease
Type IIIa affects both liver and muscle, whereas type IIIb affects the liver only
Because gluconeogenesis is intact, hypoglycaemia is typically ketotic and lactate and uric acid are usually normal, unlike type I
Serum transaminases are often markedly elevated, and hepatomegaly frequently improves after puberty
In type IIIa a progressive myopathy and cardiomyopathy can emerge in later childhood or adult life
Management centres on avoiding fasting with frequent feeds, uncooked cornstarch therapy, and a diet relatively high in protein
reference.pathophysiology: Cori disease results from deficiency of the glycogen debranching enzyme, which normally works with phosphorylase to fully degrade glycogen at its branch points. Loss of debranching activity halts glycogenolysis once the outer glucose chains are removed, leaving an abnormal glycogen molecule with short outer branches (limit dextrin) that accumulates in liver and, in type IIIa, in skeletal and cardiac muscle. Because gluconeogenesis remains functional, patients can still generate glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors, so fasting hypoglycaemia is generally milder than in type I and is accompanied by ketosis rather than lactic acidosis. Chronic glycogen and metabolic stress produce hepatomegaly and transaminitis, and in muscle-involving disease lead to progressive myopathy and cardiomyopathy.
additionalDifferentials: Glycogen storage disease type I (von Gierke)
Glycogen storage disease types VI and IX
Glycogen storage disease type IV (branching enzyme deficiency)
Other causes of ketotic hypoglycaemia in childhood
Hepatic causes of hepatomegaly with transaminitis
Muscular dystrophies or metabolic myopathies when muscle involvement predominates
additionalInvestigations: Blood glucose, ketones, lactate, and uric acid during controlled fasting
Liver function tests demonstrating elevated transaminases
Creatine kinase and cardiac assessment (echocardiography, ECG) in suspected type IIIa
Fasting studies distinguishing ketotic from lactic-acidotic hypoglycaemia
Molecular genetic testing of the AGL gene
Muscle or liver enzyme assay where diagnostic confirmation is needed
redFlags: Symptomatic hypoglycaemia with reduced consciousness or seizures
Progressive muscle weakness or exercise intolerance suggesting myopathy
Features of cardiomyopathy such as heart failure or arrhythmia in type IIIa
Progression to hepatic fibrosis or cirrhosis
reference.prognosis: Hepatic and hypoglycaemic manifestations often improve after puberty and overall prognosis is better than type I; however, in type IIIa progressive myopathy and cardiomyopathy can dominate the long-term course and determine outcome.
pitfalls: Mistaking Cori disease for von Gierke disease and expecting lactic acidosis and hyperuricaemia
Overlooking muscle and cardiac involvement in type IIIa during follow-up
Assuming hepatomegaly and transaminitis reflect primary liver disease
Neglecting cardiac surveillance in patients with muscle-affecting disease
references: Scriver's The Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
management: Dietary management is the mainstay: frequent complex-carbohydrate feeds and uncooked cornstarch, with overnight feeding in infancy, to prevent fasting ketotic hypoglycaemia
Provide a high-protein diet to exploit intact gluconeogenesis and support muscle in type IIIa
Educate on sick-day rules and emergency carbohydrate provision to avert hypoglycaemic crises during intercurrent illness
Monitor blood glucose, ketones, transaminases and creatine kinase, with growth and nutritional assessment
Undertake cardiac surveillance with echocardiography and electrocardiography for cardiomyopathy, and neuromuscular monitoring for progressive myopathy in type IIIa
Provide hepatology follow-up for liver fibrosis and adenoma surveillance
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive disorder and family screening, coordinated through a metabolic medicine multidisciplinary team
